paragraphs.source_en: The masks are one of the characteristic elements in the Round Head art; they are usually associated with the anthropomorphic figures but there are also single masks depicted, which indicates their importance as objects. Assuming that masks existed in the society producing Round Head art were also stored, it can be postulated that shelters depicting single masks could have served this purpose, among other possible functions. An example is the Uan Bender shelter in the Tassili. The richly decorated wall on the right side begins with an impressive painting of an oval mask circa 1. 5 m tall and other similar but smaller masks around it. An analogous situation is known from the Dogon culture where the Big Mask represents the first ancestor embodied in the largest and the most important mask, made only every 60 years (Palau Marti 1957).

paragraphs.source_en: It cannot be excluded that the mask at Uan Bender, because of its large dimensions, also represented a mask of special significance. Located on a hill, this shelter is hidden by surrounding rocks, suggesting a secret character. It has a roof protecting the paintings and it would also protect people and things against rain. This place would thus be suitable for the possible storing of special objects, such as the masks represented here.

paragraphs.source_en: There are many Round Head paintings representing probable dancing individuals, with or without masks, but it is impossible to state for which purposes these prehistoric people were dancing. These scenes are usually situated in shelters large enough or having enough space in front of them for a possible dancing group of people.

paragraphs.source_en: There are cases of shelters containing paintings of small dimensions and consisting usually of only a few figures. An example is Tiechiami in the Tassili, an isolated rock surrounded by a vast plain, containing four small, extremely simple static anthropomorphic figures. This site is located about 5 km from the important painted sites of Techakelaouen and Tissoukai which include numerous and large compositions, so that Tiechiami is evidently a minor site next to its more impressive neighbours. Can this simple composition of human figures represent a personal expression of a painter? The small numbers of figures, which are not repainted, suggest that the site was not one of the most important for prehistoric painters.
